notes: Monday 9 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Fri 6 – Sun 8 Nov. Economy: US jobs +165k; AI stocks bounce in US, Kospi −6%; Paraguay Ueno Bank collapse; Democrats target tariffs. Tech (USA): Nvidia probes Jensen Huang spy-link affair; Anthropic IPO vs AI backlash; Cybertruck wind-down; child-safety lawsuits. Politics: Trump 'giant step back' + Miller chief of staff; Eisenkot tasked in Israel; NZ hung result; Europe joins Abu Dhabi Ukraine talks. Literature (USA): Maas ACOTAR HOT; Queens library ransomware NOT; PW salary report NOT; Maira Kalman 'Joy' HOT. Social: Kraków shooting; Egypt train crash; Uyghurs in Thailand; Washington trans sports ban.

stories.headline: US added 165,000 jobs in October — nearly three times what experts guessed; unemployment dips to 4.1%
stories.dek: Earlier months were revised up too. Wages rose 3.1% from a year ago.
stories.caveman: Every month the US government counts how many new jobs the economy made. Experts guessed about 59,000 for October. The real number was 165,000. The unemployment rate (share of people who want work but can't find it) fell a little, to 4.1%. August and September were also revised higher. Pay went up 0.4% in one month and 3.1% over a year. One catch: a wider measure that also counts people stuck in part-time work or who gave up looking rose to 7.9%, because many more people started looking for work. Economists called it the best report in a while — a sign the economy is not falling into a slump, even with stock-market panic over AI.
stories.why_it_matters: Strong US jobs can keep interest rates higher for longer. That affects mortgage rates, the US dollar, and money flowing in and out of Asian stock markets like Taiwan's.
stories.camps: Optimists say the economy is steady and the stock drop is about AI, not a recession. Cautious voices point to the rising ‘wider’ jobless measure. Workers' groups note pay gains are still modest against living costs.
stories.image_alt: A recruiter greets a job seeker at a hiring event

terms.explain: The main monthly count of US jobs, leaving out farm work.
Share of people who want a job but don't have one.
Changed later when more complete data comes in.
Everyone who has a job or is looking for one.

stories.headline: After trillions vanish, AI stocks bounce a little in the US — but South Korea's Kospi falls 6% and Europe slides
stories.dek: Nasdaq gains 1.1% Friday after a 5.5% crash; chipmaker SK Hynix drops more than 10%.
stories.caveman: On Thursday, investors dumped tech shares, wiping out trillions of dollars of value. They feared the Democrats' big midterm win means new rules that slow down AI and the huge data centers it needs. On Friday, US markets calmed: the tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 1.1%, the S&P 500 rose 0.3%, and the Dow slipped 0.4%. Big names like Nvidia and Tesla won back some ground. But Asia and Europe had a rough Friday. South Korea's main index, the Kospi, fell 6%, and memory-chip maker SK Hynix fell over 10%. Germany, France and Spain fell too; London's FTSE 100 lost about 1%. President Trump defended AI, saying only ‘foolish leadership’ would say no to its riches.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan, Korea and Japan are the factories of the AI boom. When the US mood on AI changes, their stocks — and the pensions and savings tied to them — swing hardest.
stories.camps: Bulls say the panic was overdone and AI demand is real. Bears say AI spending got ahead of itself and politics is now catching up. Many voters say they simply want a say over data centers near their homes.
stories.image_alt: A trader watches screens on the stock exchange floor
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images / BBC

terms.explain: US stock index full of tech companies.
South Korea's main stock index.
When many investors sell at once and prices drop fast.
Giant building full of computers that power AI and the internet.

stories.headline: Paraguay bank collapse freezes accounts for 60% of adults — and topples the president
stories.dek: Digital lender Ueno Bank failed; ex-president Santiago Peña is charged and under house arrest.
stories.caveman: Ueno Bank was a phone-app bank in Paraguay (a country in South America). It grew super fast, offered high returns, and even sponsored the national football team. Last week the central bank shut it down for being insolvent — it owed more than it had. Overnight, nearly 3 million people — about 60% of adults — could not reach their money. Some businesses say sales fell up to 80%. President Santiago Peña, accused of favoring the bank, resigned, hoping to keep a lifetime Senate seat that protects ex-presidents. Lawmakers took that seat away anyway. Prosecutors charged him with ‘breach of trust’ and asked to hold him in custody; he is under house arrest. One customer said he now has to ‘work miracles’ to pay bills.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how one fast-growing app bank can become ‘too big to fail’ in a small country. Paraguay is also one of Taiwan's few remaining diplomatic allies; Taiwan says ties are not affected.
stories.camps: Critics say Peña's government let Ueno grow with too little oversight. His allies call the charges political. Ordinary savers mostly want one thing: their money back.
stories.image_alt: Santiago Peña signs his resignation letter in Asunción
stories.image_credit: Photo: Laura Fioravanti/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: Owing more money than you have; can't pay debts.
A country's top money authority; it watches over banks.
Being forced to stay at home instead of jail while a case goes on.
Misusing power or money that people trusted you with.

stories.headline: Democrats plan to go after Trump's tariffs first — especially the trade war with Canada
stories.dek: New House majority wants votes to take back Congress's power over tariffs, plus investigations into tariff exemptions.
stories.caveman: Tariffs are taxes on goods brought in from other countries. For two years President Trump used them a lot, on his own authority. Democrats, who will control Congress from January, say these tariffs make life more expensive. Their plan has two parts. First: a ‘first 100 hours’ burst of bills, including ones that give Congress back its power over trade. Hakeem Jeffries, likely the next House Speaker, calls ending Trump's tariffs a top priority. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan says ending the Canada trade war must happen ‘immediately.’ Second: investigations. Democrat Jamie Raskin has asked for records on which companies got special tariff exemptions, suggesting favors for Trump allies. Trump can still veto bills, so a fight is coming.
stories.why_it_matters: US tariffs shape prices worldwide and decide how much Taiwan's companies pay to sell to America. A change here would hit factories and supply chains across Asia.
stories.camps: Democrats say tariffs are a hidden tax on families. Trump and allies say tariffs protect US jobs and are leverage in deals. Some economists say undoing tariffs quickly could still be messy for businesses.
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images / CNBC

terms.explain: A tax on goods imported from another country.
When the president refuses to sign a bill, blocking it unless Congress overrides.
Special permission not to follow a rule or pay a tax.
The leader of the US House of Representatives.

stories.headline: Nvidia opens probe into CEO Jensen Huang after he admits affair with woman US agencies call a Chinese spy
stories.dek: Board says it sees no sign secrets leaked; lawmakers from both parties want answers by Nov 18.
stories.caveman: Jensen Huang runs Nvidia, the company that makes the chips most AI runs on — one of the most valuable firms on Earth. He was born in Taiwan. Reports in The New York Times and Financial Times say US intelligence believes a businesswoman named Alice Huang, linked to an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, was passing information to China. On Sunday, Jensen Huang emailed staff: he admitted he had an affair with her, apologized to his family, and said the board had opened an independent investigation. The board says it has ‘no reason to believe’ national security or company secrets were compromised. Megaspeed has been accused of helping restricted Chinese firms get Nvidia chips. Three House Republican committee chairs want a closed-door briefing on Nov 18; Democratic Senator Chris Coons promises his own investigation.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of the US–China tech fight and depends heavily on TSMC in Taiwan. Questions about its boss could affect chip export rules and the AI supply chain.
stories.camps: Nvidia says no secrets were shared and Huang stays CEO. Critics in both parties ask whether China tried to sway US chip policy through him. Some warn against judging before the investigation ends.

terms.explain: Group that oversees a company's leaders on behalf of shareholders.
Government rules limiting which products can be sold to certain countries.
A private meeting with lawmakers, not open to the public.
Government spy and security services, like the CIA or FBI.

stories.headline: Anthropic's giant IPO walks into an AI backlash: voters said no to 40 of 41 data-center ballot measures
stories.dek: Investors now see a $1–1.5 trillion value, down from $2 trillion talk; Nasdaq debut likely mid-November.
stories.caveman: Anthropic is the AI company behind the Claude chatbot. It plans to sell shares to the public for the first time (an IPO), probably on the Nasdaq in mid-November. But the mood has changed fast. In last week's US elections, voters showed distrust of tech billionaires and AI. Candidates who wanted tougher AI rules won in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia. Local communities voted against data-center-related measures in 40 of 41 cases. An NBC exit poll found more than half of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote. Investors now talk about valuing Anthropic at $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from $2 trillion. A behavioral scientist told CNBC a huge-valuation IPO feeds the ‘big tech billionaire’ image people dislike.
stories.why_it_matters: How this IPO goes will show whether money keeps pouring into AI. That money buys chips and servers — many made in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Supporters say Anthropic has positioned itself as safety-focused and still has strong demand. Skeptics say the price is a ‘stretch’ in a falling market. Community groups say AI firms must earn local trust for data centers, power and water.
stories.image_alt: AI executive speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos

terms.explain: Initial public offering: when a private company first sells shares to the public.
How much investors think a whole company is worth.
A question voters decide directly, like a local rule or law.
A survey of voters right after they vote.

stories.headline: Musk says Tesla will wind down the Cybertruck in Texas by mid-2027 to make room for robotaxis
stories.dek: US sales fell 48% last year; SpaceX itself bought $131 million worth of the steel trucks.
stories.caveman: The Cybertruck is Tesla's sharp-edged steel pickup truck. Elon Musk once predicted 250,000 sales a year. It never came close. Researchers at Cox Automotive estimate about 20,000 were sold in the US last year — down 48% from 2024. One big buyer was Musk's own rocket company, SpaceX, which spent $131 million on them. Now Musk says Tesla will ‘wind down’ Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of next year, to build the Cybercab — a two-seat self-driving taxi with no steering wheel. He didn't say if the truck will be made anywhere else, but said the existing Cybertrucks ‘will be around for a long time.’
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how hype and real demand can be very different. Tesla is betting its future on robotaxis, which still face safety and legal questions.
stories.camps: Fans call the Cybertruck bold and loved. Critics call it an expensive flop. Investors are split on whether robotaxis are Tesla's next big win or another overpromise.

terms.explain: Slowly reduce and then stop.
A taxi that drives itself with no human driver.
Tesla's name for its giant factories.

stories.headline: Snap settles to keep its CEO off the stand as child-safety lawsuits pile up — while Big Tech pushes AI into classrooms
stories.dek: Meta and YouTube already lost a social-media injury trial this year; more trials start in March.
stories.caveman: Many US families are suing social-media companies, saying apps were designed to hook kids and harmed their mental health. Earlier this year, Meta and YouTube lost a big jury trial. This week Snap (maker of Snapchat) settled one related case, so CEO Evan Spiegel did not have to testify in a Los Angeles court. A lawyer told CNBC these settlements show companies trying to avoid public trials as their reputations take hits. At the same time, Google, Meta and AI firms are pushing AI tools into schools. A child-development psychologist said safety must be built in from the start, ‘not after the fact.’ More trials are set for March.
stories.why_it_matters: Kids everywhere, including in Taiwan, use the same apps. US court cases often push companies to change product design worldwide.
stories.camps: Parents and advocates say companies knew the risks and must pay. Tech firms say they've added safety tools and that settling is not admitting guilt. Teachers are split on AI in class: helpful tutor or new distraction.

terms.explain: End a lawsuit by agreeing to a deal, usually paying money, before a verdict.
A trial where ordinary citizens decide the outcome.
Answer questions under oath in court.
How much time and attention users give an app.

stories.headline: Trump says America took a ‘giant step back’ after Republican midterm losses; hardliner Stephen Miller becomes chief of staff today
stories.dek: Trump offers UFC boss Dana White the press secretary job; his attorney general hints at probes of Democrats.
stories.caveman: Last Tuesday, Republicans lost control of both houses of Congress. On Sunday, President Trump posted that America ‘took a giant step back in History’ and promised to come back ‘bigger and stronger.’ Instead of moving to the middle, he seems to be moving further right. Stephen Miller, a hardline aide known for tough immigration policies, starts as White House chief of staff on Monday. Trump also offered Dana White, head of the fighting league UFC, the job of press secretary. When Democrats said they would investigate the administration, Trump said he told the Justice Department to ‘look into’ them; Attorney General Todd Blanche said ‘there could be’ investigations, without naming any crime. Democrats say Miller and Elon Musk will likely be investigated by Congress from January.
stories.why_it_matters: A president fighting a hostile Congress can mean gridlock, government shutdown threats, and more use of executive power — all of which ripple into world trade and security, including US policy on Taiwan.
stories.camps: Trump allies say he must fight, not surrender, to a ‘radical’ Congress. Democrats say voters rejected his agenda and threats against lawmakers are dangerous. Some Republicans quietly worry a bunker strategy will cost them in 2028.
stories.image_credit: Photo: Eric Lee/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: The president's top aide who runs the White House team.
The White House spokesperson who talks to reporters.
Congress checking and investigating what the government does.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.

stories.headline: Israel's president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a government after deadlocked election
stories.dek: Eisenkot's bloc has 48 of 120 seats, Netanyahu's 53; both Arab-majority parties back Eisenkot.
stories.caveman: In Israel, no party usually wins a majority alone, so parties team up to reach 61 of 120 seats. After the 27 October election, nobody got there. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's religious-nationalist camp won 53 seats; the opposition led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar party) won 48. President Isaac Herzog chose Eisenkot to try first, partly because both Arab-majority parties — which made record gains — endorsed him. Eisenkot called for a ‘national emergency government.’ His paths are hard: share power with Netanyahu, rely on Arab-led parties (some of his allies refuse), or deal with ultra-Orthodox parties who demand their community be exempt from military service. If he succeeds, he would replace Israel's longest-serving leader.
stories.why_it_matters: Who leads Israel affects the wars and ceasefires in Gaza and with Iran — and with them, oil prices and global security.
stories.camps: Eisenkot's supporters want change after years of Netanyahu and war. Netanyahu's camp says it is still the biggest bloc. Arab parties see a rare chance to shape government; some Jewish nationalist voters reject that idea.
stories.image_credit: Photo: Paulina Patimer/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: Several parties joining together to make a majority and govern.
A group of parties on the same side.
Very strictly religious Jewish communities.
A small group whose support decides who wins power.

stories.headline: New Zealand election ends with no clear winner; newcomer Qiulae Wong's centrist party could decide who governs
stories.dek: Final count not until 27 November; ‘who won the election’ was New Zealand's top Google search.
stories.caveman: New Zealand voted on Saturday. Neither the center-right National Party of Prime Minister Christopher Luxon nor the center-left Labour Party of Chris Hipkins won enough seats. Voters, tired of economic troubles and unexcited by both leaders, gave more votes to smaller parties. A surprise: the Opportunity party, led by 38-year-old political newcomer Qiulae Wong, won about seven seats. She promises ‘evidence-based centrism’ and says she could work with either side. That makes her a possible kingmaker. Talks to form a government won't really start until final results come out on 27 November, so it may be weeks before New Zealanders know their next leader.
stories.why_it_matters: It's part of a global trend: voters drifting away from big traditional parties toward newcomers and smaller groups.
stories.camps: National says it's still best placed to lead. Labour says voters punished the government. Supporters of small parties say their stronger voice will force big parties to compromise.
stories.image_alt: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addresses supporters in Auckland

terms.explain: Moderate conservative / moderate progressive.
A smaller political party that usually wins few seats.
Politics in the middle, mixing ideas from left and right.

stories.headline: Europe says it will join US-brokered Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi this week, despite Kremlin saying no
stories.dek: Trump hints a deal ‘might involve all of Europe’; Zelenskyy warns of a new ‘Yalta.’
stories.caveman: The US is hosting peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi (in the United Arab Emirates) on Tuesday and Wednesday. They were supposed to be three-way: US, Russia, Ukraine. Russia's spokesman said Europe had no role. But France's foreign minister said Sunday, ‘France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard.’ It's unclear whether Europeans will negotiate or only observe. After meeting a Kremlin envoy, President Trump said the coming deal is ‘going to involve more than Ukraine’ and ‘might involve all of Europe.’ Ukraine's President Zelenskyy said he hadn't been told the details and compared it to the 1945 Yalta conference, where big powers decided Europe's borders without asking smaller countries. Russian missile strikes hit Kyiv again on Saturday.
stories.why_it_matters: How this war ends will shape whether big countries can take land by force — something Taiwan watches closely.
stories.camps: Europe says it can't be left out of decisions about its own security. Russia wants a deal with Washington alone. Ukraine fears being pressured into giving up land. Trump says he wants the war over fast.
stories.image_alt: Bomb crater seen through the destroyed walls of a kindergarten in Kyiv

terms.explain: Russia's government (named after its seat of power in Moscow).
Help two sides reach a deal as a go-between.
1945 meeting where the US, UK and Soviet Union divided postwar Europe.
An official sent to represent a government in talks.

stories.headline: HOT: Sarah J. Maas's new ACOTAR book sells 958,000 hardcovers in one week — the biggest debut of 2026
stories.dek: A Court of Splintered Harmony outsold the next 78 bestsellers combined; another Maas novel lands January 12.
stories.caveman: Sarah J. Maas writes ‘romantasy’ — romance mixed with fantasy. Her series A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) is hugely popular, especially with young women on BookTok. The newest book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, came out October 27 and sold 958,195 hardcover copies in its first week in the US, according to sales tracker Circana BookScan. That's more than the next 78 books on the Publishers Weekly bestseller list put together, and the biggest first week of the year. It is already the fourth best-selling book of 2026. Her publisher, Bloomsbury, which had a weak first half, is counting on her. The next book, A Court of Forgotten Melody, comes out January 12, 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows who really drives book sales now: genre fiction and online fan communities, not just prize-winning literary novels.
stories.camps: Fans say romantasy gets readers, especially teens, excited about books. Some critics dismiss it as formula. Booksellers mostly just say thank you — one author can keep a whole publisher afloat.
stories.image_alt: A Court of Splintered Harmony by Sarah J. Maas

terms.explain: Books that mix romance and fantasy.
Service that counts how many print books are sold in stores.
A book with a hard, stiff cover — usually the first, pricier edition.
Older books a publisher still sells.

stories.headline: NOT: Queens Public Library's whole online system held for ransom by hackers
stories.dek: 66 branches stay open, but Wi-Fi, computers, the app and e-books are down; staff go back to manual checkout.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday, November 4, hackers attacked the online network of the Queens Public Library in New York City, which runs 66 branches. Everything digital went offline: the website, public computers, self-checkout machines, Wi-Fi, the app, and e-books. The hackers are demanding a ransom — money to unlock it. Nobody has said how much or who did it. It's also unknown if users' personal information was stolen. The library's CEO said it is ‘a victim of the type of world we're living in.’ Branches are still open, and librarians check books in and out by hand. Lit Hub's writer, a Queens native, was furious: libraries give books, internet and classes to people for free, in one of the most diverse places in the world.
stories.why_it_matters: For many people, the library is their only free internet and computer. Attacks on public services hurt the poorest most.
stories.camps: Everyone agrees attacking a library is low. Security experts say public institutions are easy targets because they lack money for cybersecurity. Some argue governments should fund protection for libraries, schools and hospitals.

terms.explain: Malicious software that locks your files until you pay.
One local location of a larger library system.
An attempt to break into or damage computer systems.

stories.headline: NOT so hot: US publishing pay slips — median salary $78,000 — and workers who use AI the most like it the least
stories.dek: Publishers Weekly's annual survey of 886 people: 3% raises, high job satisfaction, but few promotions.
stories.caveman: Every year, Publishers Weekly asks people who work in US book publishing about their pay and jobs. This year 886 people answered. The median salary (the middle number) was $78,000, down from $80,000 in 2024. Most got only a modest raise of about 3%. About 80% of workers are women. The share of new workers who are not white fell a bit, which some link to the Trump administration's pushback against diversity programs. Still, 60% said they are very satisfied with their jobs; the biggest complaint is that there's little chance to move up. On AI: 73% said their company uses AI somehow, mostly for market research — but the more people use it, the less they like it, and many worry about AI's effect on their jobs.
stories.why_it_matters: The people who choose, edit and sell books shape what we all get to read. Low pay can push out people without family money, making books less diverse.
stories.camps: Some publishers say tight budgets limit raises. Workers and unions say low pay is why talent leaves. Opinions on AI split: useful helper for data tasks, or a threat to creative jobs.

terms.explain: The middle value when numbers are lined up from low to high.
Diversity, equity and inclusion — programs to include more kinds of people.
Black, Indigenous and people of color.

stories.headline: HOT: Maira Kalman's new book ‘Joy’ argues you can't have joy without sorrow
stories.dek: The New York painter-author's gouache paintings go on show at Mary Ryan Gallery this month.
stories.caveman: Maira Kalman is a beloved New York artist and author of more than 30 books, known for colorful, playful paintings with short, funny, wise words. Her new book is simply called ‘Joy.’ She worried it would be a hard sell in dark times. Her morning routine: coffee and reading the obituaries — it gives ‘a sense of proportion,’ she told NPR. Then she walks around Manhattan looking for small moments that make her heart stop. The book shows a woman putting on red lipstick in Paris, a man playing violin under a cherry tree, and a swimmer coming up for air. Most of the text is questions. Her big idea: ‘You cannot be joyous without sorrow.’ The paintings are on show at the Mary Ryan Gallery in New York this month.
stories.why_it_matters: In a heavy news season, a book about noticing small joys is getting attention — and it's a reminder that art books can be both light and deep.
stories.camps: Fans find her work comforting and honest. Some readers find whimsy too sweet for hard times; Kalman's answer is that joy and sorrow live side by side.

terms.explain: A thick, matte watercolor-like paint.
A news notice about someone who has died, often telling their life story.
Playful, quirky humor.

stories.headline: Kraków shooting: gunman kills six in old-town square; Poland opens terrorism probe into far-right suspect
stories.dek: The 24-year-old's parents and sister were found dead at home; two days of national mourning.
stories.caveman: On Saturday afternoon, a 24-year-old man wearing military-style clothes and a bulletproof vest drove into Kraków's main square — packed with tourists — and started shooting at random. Six people were killed, including a 32-year-old British man and a 51-year-old Austrian woman; 17 were hurt, including two police officers. Police wounded and arrested him. Later, police found his father, mother and sister dead at the family home about 100 miles away. Poland's interior minister said the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideas and held ‘ultra-nationalistic’ views. Prosecutors are treating it as terrorism. Mass shootings are rare in Poland; the country is now in two days of mourning, and people leave candles in the square.
stories.why_it_matters: It adds to worries across Europe about young people being radicalized online by extremist content.
stories.camps: Officials call for more action against online extremism. Some politicians focus on gun access; others on mental health and policing. Victims' families ask for answers on how warning signs were missed.
stories.image_alt: People mourn near the scene of the shooting in Kraków
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: Violence meant to scare people for a political or ideological goal.
Extreme nationalist politics, often hostile to immigrants or minorities.
Pushed toward extreme beliefs, often through online content.
Official days when a country honors victims.

stories.headline: Two trains collide near Giza, Egypt: at least seven dead, more than 100 injured
stories.dek: A train to Fayoum hit the back of a stopped Cairo–Aswan train; carriages fell down an embankment.
stories.caveman: On Sunday, two trains heading south from Giza and Cairo collided in Egypt. A train going from Giza to Fayoum crashed into the back of another train that was stopped on the tracks on its way to Aswan. Several carriages flipped and rolled down a slope; one looked split in two. At least seven people died, including one of the train drivers, and more than 100 were hurt, mostly with broken bones and head injuries. Prosecutors warned the death toll could rise. President Sisi ordered an investigation and said anyone negligent will be held accountable. The crash happened near the site of Egypt's worst train disaster, a 2002 fire that killed more than 370 people.
stories.why_it_matters: Egypt's railways carry millions of poorer people who can't afford other transport. Repeated crashes raise questions about safety spending.
stories.camps: The government points to big rail upgrades in recent years. Critics say old signals and poor maintenance still put passengers at risk. Families want accountability, not just inquiries.
stories.image_alt: People search derailed train carriages near Giza

terms.explain: When a train comes off its tracks.
A raised bank of earth that tracks or roads run on.
Careless in a way that causes harm.

stories.headline: Two Uyghur men fear Thailand will send them back to China, where they say they'll be ‘like slaves’
stories.dek: Last year Thailand deported 40 Uyghur men despite UN pleas; rights groups urge a safe third country.
stories.caveman: Uyghurs are a mostly Muslim ethnic group in western China. The UN has said China's crackdown on them may be a crime against humanity. In 2014, more than 200 Uyghurs fled China and were caught in Thailand. Women and children were later sent to Turkey, but the men were sent back to China in groups. Last year Thailand deported 40 of them, even though the US and Canada reportedly offered to take them; their whereabouts are still unknown, the UN says. Now two more men, just moved to an immigration detention center after a prison term, fear they are next. One told his girlfriend he wants to go ‘anywhere else but China.’ Human Rights Watch says Thailand should let them go to a safe third country.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a test of whether smaller countries will bow to Beijing's pressure on human rights. Taiwan faces similar Chinese pressure on its partners.
stories.camps: Rights groups say deportation could mean torture or disappearance. Thailand has said it follows its laws and diplomatic relations. China says Uyghur policy is about security and calls criticism interference.
stories.image_alt: Illustration: letters from Uyghur men at risk of deportation
stories.image_credit: Photo: Guardian Pictures/EPA via The Guardian

terms.explain: A mostly Muslim Turkic ethnic group from Xinjiang, western China.
Forcing someone to leave a country.
Very serious, widespread attacks on civilians, under international law.
A different country that agrees to take refugees.

stories.headline: ‘The blue wave isn't applicable to trans people’: Washington state voters approve school sports ban; advocates prepare lawsuit
stories.dek: Initiative 638 requires girls to ‘verify biological sex’; opponents warn of invasive exams.
stories.caveman: While Democrats won big across the US last week, voters in Washington state — long a safe haven for transgender people — approved Initiative 638. It bans transgender girls from girls' school sports and takes effect next month. The text says all girls in school sports must ‘verify biological sex,’ which can include confirming ‘reproductive anatomy.’ Opponents say that could force tens of thousands of girls into invasive body checks. A coalition of advocacy groups plans to sue in state courts, citing Washington's strong privacy and anti-discrimination laws. The same conservative group, Let's Go Washington, lost its two other ballot measures this year, including one to repeal a tax on high earners.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows that voters can lean left on economics and still back limits on trans rights — and that courts are now the main battlefield.
stories.camps: Supporters say the ban is about fairness and safety in girls' sports. Opponents say it singles out a tiny group of kids and invades all girls' privacy. Legal experts expect a long court fight.
stories.image_alt: A No Hate in Washington State rally in Seattle
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lindsey Wasson/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: A person whose gender identity is different from the sex they were assigned at birth.
A law proposed by citizens and decided by a public vote.
A place where people are protected from harm.
A big election win for Democrats (whose color is blue).
